messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 46
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Graphic Designer
  trauma_type: Police
  pcl5: 65

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Intrusive Thoughts: Unwanted thoughts, Visual (Injuries): Visible injuries or wounds on others, Authority Presence: Police
  Maladaptive Strategies: Screen Escape: I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking, Avoid People: avoid other people, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time
  Threat: Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Memory: Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it

Vignette:
Michael was 46, a married graphic designer from a European American family, and when he first came to treatment he described his life as if it had been split cleanly in two: before the police encounter and after it. The event itself had taken place during what should have been an ordinary evening. He had been stopped by police, and what began as a tense interaction escalated into a frightening scene in which he was left exposed to authority figures he could not reason with or get away from. He did not describe every detail in a tidy sequence; instead, when he tried to tell it, he would lose the thread partway through, stopping and starting as if the memory itself pulled him under. What stayed with him most vividly were flashes of visible injuries and wounds on others nearby, sights that lodged in him with a force he had not expected. Even now, if he tried to explain what had happened, he often found himself unable to finish, his voice trailing off as the feeling of it became too much to hold and speak at the same time.

In the months that followed, Michael noticed that the memory could arrive without warning. He might be at home, in the middle of a normal task, and something in the surroundings would suddenly bring back the full scene so quickly that he would have to stop what he was doing. He described the return of the memory as overwhelming, not just upsetting, but so flooded with emotion that he had to cut himself off from it. He became especially wary of police presence; even seeing officers in person, on television, or outside his window could make him feel instantly on edge. The sight of injuries on other people carried the same charge. A scraped knee, a cut hand, or blood visible on someone else could jolt him back into that night in a way that felt immediate and physical, as if his body had already started responding before he had a chance to think. He said he hated that this could happen anywhere, at any time, and that he never knew what ordinary object or image might suddenly open the door to the memory.

Living with that unpredictability changed the way Michael moved through the world. He had come to avoid other people more than he used to, keeping his contact limited and creating distance whenever he could. At work as a graphic designer, he increasingly structured his day around remaining mentally occupied, filling every gap with tasks so there was no quiet moment for his mind to drift. Outside of work, he spent long hours on his phone, on games, or scrolling the internet, not because he enjoyed all of it, but because being absorbed in a screen made it easier to keep the unwanted thoughts from breaking through. He no longer felt comfortable in many places unless he had first identified escape routes and checked how he would get out if he needed to leave quickly. In restaurants, meeting rooms, and even in his own house, he would take in doors, hallways, and exits before he could settle enough to sit down. He said he knew, intellectually, that he was in safe places, but he was unable to relax there anyway. His body stayed tense and ready, as if it had not received the message that the danger was over.

Over time, Michael’s sense of what his life was supposed to mean became badly shaken. He spoke with a hard, flat conviction that nothing in his life felt meaningful anymore and that the trauma had destroyed the life he thought he had been living before. What angered and haunted him just as much was his belief that what had happened to him had been deeply unfair and that nothing had been done about it. He carried that injustice with him, revisiting it in his mind with no sense that it had been answered or made right. Although he remained married, the pattern of withdrawing, staying on his phone, and avoiding people had changed the atmosphere at home, leaving his wife frustrated by how difficult it was to reach him. By the time he sought help, it was not because the memories had vanished but because they had become impossible to keep managing alone. He wanted relief from the constant state of alertness and from the way the memory could seize him so completely, and he was most afraid that this would remain the rest of his life—that he would never again feel safe enough to let his body stand down, never mind feel that his life meant anything at all.
